claim: EMC1 is a member of the ER membrane protein complex (EMC).
source: We find that a member of the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) called EMC1 promotes SV40 ER membrane transport and infection.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a factual description of EMC1's identity.

claim: EMC1 promotes SV40 ER membrane transport.
source: We find that a member of the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) called EMC1 promotes SV40 ER membrane transport and infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D demonstrating EMC1 depletion blocks SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport.

claim: EMC1 promotes SV40 infection.
source: We find that a member of the ER membrane protein complex (EMC) called EMC1 promotes SV40 ER membrane transport and infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating EMC1 knockdown reduces SV40 infection.

claim: EMC1 uses its predicted transmembrane residue D961 to bind to SV40.
source: Surprisingly, EMC1 does so by using its predicted transmembrane residue D961 to bind to and stabilize the membrane-embedded partially destabilized SV40, thereby preventing premature viral disassembly.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B showing D961A mutant has reduced SV40 binding.

claim: EMC1 stabilizes membrane-embedded partially destabilized SV40.
source: Surprisingly, EMC1 does so by using its predicted transmembrane residue D961 to bind to and stabilize the membrane-embedded partially destabilized SV40, thereby preventing premature viral disassembly.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing SV40 disassembles prematurely when EMC1 is depleted.

claim: EMC1 prevents premature viral disassembly of SV40.
source: Surprisingly, EMC1 does so by using its predicted transmembrane residue D961 to bind to and stabilize the membrane-embedded partially destabilized SV40, thereby preventing premature viral disassembly.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6A showing disassembled virus appears in EMC1-depleted cells.

claim: EMC1-dependent stabilization enables SV40 to engage a cytosolic extraction complex.
source: EMC1-dependent stabilization enables SV40 to engage a cytosolic extraction complex that ejects the virus into the cytosol.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing SV40 cannot bind to Hsc70 or SGTA when EMC1 is depleted.

claim: The cytosolic extraction complex ejects SV40 into the cytosol.
source: EMC1-dependent stabilization enables SV40 to engage a cytosolic extraction complex that ejects the virus into the cytosol.
evidence: Based on previous studies cited and inference from the membrane transport assay results.

claim: EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone.
source: Thus EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, bracing the destabilized SV40 in a transport-competent state.
evidence: Inferred from the stabilization function and binding data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Coordinated destabilization-stabilization drives membrane transport of a non-enveloped virus.
source: Our findings reveal the novel principle that coordinated destabilization-stabilization drives membrane transport of a non-enveloped virus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing both destabilization and stabilization are required.

claim: BK, JC, and Merkel cell PyV cause debilitating and fatal human diseases.
source: Because PyV family members, including the human BK, JC, and Merkel cell PyV, cause debilitating and fatal human diseases, clarifying the precise molecular basis of this decisive infection step should advance our efforts to develop more effective therapies against PyV-induced human diseases (DeCaprio and Garcea, 2013; Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SV40 is the archetype PyV.
source: Simian virus 40 (SV40) is the archetype PyV, displaying both genetic and structural similarity to human PyVs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SV40 displays genetic and structural similarity to human PyVs.
source: Simian virus 40 (SV40) is the archetype PyV, displaying both genetic and structural similarity to human PyVs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SV40 consists of 360 copies of the major coat protein VP1 arranged as 72 pentamers.
source: Structurally, SV40 consists of 360 copies of the major coat protein VP1 arranged as 72 pentamers (Stehle et al., 1996; Liddington et al., 1991), with each pentamer encapsulating an internal hydrophobic protein VP2 or VP3 (Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Each SV40 VP1 pentamer encapsulates an internal hydrophobic protein VP2 or VP3.
source: Structurally, SV40 consists of 360 copies of the major coat protein VP1 arranged as 72 pentamers (Stehle et al., 1996; Liddington et al., 1991), with each pentamer encapsulating an internal hydrophobic protein VP2 or VP3 (Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to structural study.

claim: The assembled SV40 pentamers form a viral particle of approximately 45 nm in diameter.
source: The assembled pentamers form a viral particle of approximately 45 nm in diameter, which encases the 5 kilobase DNA genome.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about SV40.

claim: SV40 encases a 5 kilobase DNA genome.
source: The assembled pentamers form a viral particle of approximately 45 nm in diameter, which encases the 5 kilobase DNA genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SV40 genome size.

claim: SV40's disulfide bonds provide critical structural support for the viral particle.
source: SV40's disulfide bonds provide critical structural support for the viral particle, while the VP1 C-terminal arms invade neighboring pentamers to further stabilize the overall viral architecture (Stehle et al., 1996; Liddington et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: VP1 C-terminal arms invade neighboring pentamers to stabilize the viral architecture.
source: SV40's disulfide bonds provide critical structural support for the viral particle, while the VP1 C-terminal arms invade neighboring pentamers to further stabilize the overall viral architecture (Stehle et al., 1996; Liddington et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Calcium ions bound to SV40 strengthen inter-pentamer interactions.
source: Additionally, calcium ions bound to SV40 strengthens inter-pentamer interactions (Stehle et al., 1996; Liddington et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: SV40 traffics from the cell surface to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: To infect cells, SV40 traffics from the cell surface to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Gilbert and Benjamin, 2004; Qian et al., 2009; Kartenbeck et al., 1989) where it penetrates the ER membrane to reach the cytosol (Inoue and Tsai, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to trafficking studies.

claim: SV40 penetrates the ER membrane to reach the cytosol.
source: To infect cells, SV40 traffics from the cell surface to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Gilbert and Benjamin, 2004; Qian et al., 2009; Kartenbeck et al., 1989) where it penetrates the ER membrane to reach the cytosol (Inoue and Tsai, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: SV40 transports into the nucleus where transcription and replication of the viral genome lead to lytic infection or cellular transformation.
source: The virus then transports into the nucleus where transcription and replication of the viral genome lead to lytic infection or cellular transformation (Nakanishi et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Destabilization of the viral particle is essential to promote SV40 membrane translocation.
source: Although SV40 ER-to-cytosol membrane penetration remains enigmatic, a key concept has nonetheless emerged: destabilization of the viral particle is essential to promote membrane translocation.
evidence: This is a concept established by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: PDI and ERdj5 isomerize and reduce SV40's disulfide bonds upon reaching the ER.
source: Specifically, upon reaching the ER, protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) family members including PDI and ERdj5 isomerize and reduce SV40's disulfide bonds (Schelhaas et al., 2007; Inoue et al., 2015); for the murine PyV and possibly JC PyV, another non-catalytically active PDI family member ERp29 locally unfolds the VP1 C-terminal arm (Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ERp29 locally unfolds the VP1 C-terminal arm for murine PyV and possibly JC PyV.
source: Specifically, upon reaching the ER, protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) family members including PDI and ERdj5 isomerize and reduce SV40's disulfide bonds (Schelhaas et al., 2007; Inoue et al., 2015); for the murine PyV and possibly JC PyV, another non-catalytically active PDI family member ERp29 locally unfolds the VP1 C-terminal arm (Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disulfide bond reduction and VP1 C-terminal arm unfolding disrupt the viral architecture, exposing hydrophobic proteins VP2 and VP3.
source: These reactions disrupt the viral architecture, exposing its hydrophobic proteins VP2 and VP3 (Magnuson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The destabilized hydrophobic SV40 binds to and integrates into the ER membrane.
source: The resulting destabilized hydrophobic virus in turn binds to and integrates into the ER membrane (Norkin et al., 2002; Rainey-Barger et al., 2007; Kuksin and Norkin, 2012; Daniels et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Hsp70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery extracts membrane-embedded SV40 into the cytosol.
source: When the membrane-embedded virus becomes exposed to the cytosol, it likely experiences further destabilization as it is extracted into the cytosol by the cytosolic Hsp70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015), which is tethered to ER membrane J-proteins including DNAJ C18, as well as DNAJ B12 and B14 (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015; Goodwin et al., 2011; Bagchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Hsp70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery is tethered to ER membrane J-proteins including DNAJ C18, B12, and B14.
source: When the membrane-embedded virus becomes exposed to the cytosol, it likely experiences further destabilization as it is extracted into the cytosol by the cytosolic Hsp70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015), which is tethered to ER membrane J-proteins including DNAJ C18, as well as DNAJ B12 and B14 (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015; Goodwin et al., 2011; Bagchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Three ER membrane J-proteins C18, B12, and B14 execute important yet non-overlapping roles during SV40 ER membrane penetration.
source: Previous studies found that three ER membrane J-proteins C18, B12, and B14 execute important yet non-overlapping roles during SV40 ER membrane penetration (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015; Goodwin et al., 2011; Bagchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EMC1 is identified as a C18 binding partner by mass spectrometry.
source: The results identified potential C18 interacting partners (Figure 1A, silver stained gel), including an approximately 110 kDa protein called ER membrane protein complex subunit 1 (EMC1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: EMC1 is predicted to be a single-pass type I ER-resident transmembrane protein.
source: EMC1 is predicted to be a single-pass type I ER-resident transmembrane protein that is the largest component of a multiprotein complex called ER membrane protein complex (EMC), which consists of 10 proteins in humans (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study describing EMC structure.

claim: EMC1 is the largest component of the ER membrane protein complex (EMC).
source: EMC1 is predicted to be a single-pass type I ER-resident transmembrane protein that is the largest component of a multiprotein complex called ER membrane protein complex (EMC), which consists of 10 proteins in humans (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The EMC consists of 10 proteins in humans.
source: EMC1 is predicted to be a single-pass type I ER-resident transmembrane protein that is the largest component of a multiprotein complex called ER membrane protein complex (EMC), which consists of 10 proteins in humans (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The EMC was previously implicated in ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
source: Because the EMC was previously implicated in an ER-to-cytosol transport pathway called ER-associated degradation (ERAD) (Christianson et al., 2012; Jonikas et al., 2009; Ruggiano et al., 2014), we focused this study on EMC1 because SV40 similarly undergoes ER-to-cytosol transport.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: C18 binds to Hsc70.
source: To validate the mass spectrometry data, the same samples were subjected to SDS-PAGE following by immunoblotting using a specific antibody against EMC1, which confirmed the identity of this protein (Figure 1B, top panel); as expected, C18 also binds to Hsc70 (Figure 1B, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Shot-gun mass spectrometry identified peptides corresponding to EMC2, EMC3, EMC4, EMC6, and EMC10 in C18 precipitates.
source: When the entire precipitated material prepared from C18-expressing and control parental cells were subjected to 'shot-gun' mass spectrometry analyses, in addition to peptides matching EMC1, peptides corresponding to EMC2, EMC3, EMC4, EMC6, and EMC10 were also identified (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: C18 preferentially binds to EMC1 compared to B14 and B12.
source: To test if EMC1 displays preferential binding to the three ER membrane J-proteins C18, B14, and B12, HEK 293T cells were transfected with either GFP containing a S-tag (GFP-S) or a S-tagged form of the J-proteins. The transfected cells were lysed, followed by affinity purification (AP) with S-agarose beads. When the samples were subjected to SDS-PAGE followed by immunoblotting, only C18 significantly pulled down endogenous EMC1 (Figure 1C, top panel, compare lane 2 to 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The C18-EMC1 interaction is observed in COS-7 cells.
source: The C18-EMC1 interaction was also observed in COS-7 cells (Figure 1D), which is a simian cell line derived from the parental CV-1 cells that affords a high transfection efficiency; simian CV-1 cells are typically used to study SV40 entry.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Depleting EMC1 using siRNA does not affect the levels of B14, B12, C18, BAP31, or Derlin-1.
source: Immunoblotting of the resulting whole cell extract (WCE) confirmed that EMC1 was largely depleted in cells transfected with the EMC1-specific siRNAs (Figure 2A, top panel), while the levels of the single-pass B14/B12/C18 (Figure 2A, second, third, and fourth panels) or multi-pass BAP31/Derlin-1 (Figure 2A, fifth and sixth panels) membrane proteins were largely unaffected.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depleting EMC1 does not induce ER stress.
source: We found that depleting EMC1 using either siRNAs did not generate the spliced form of the XBP1 mRNA [XBP1 (s)], in contrast to cells treated with the chemical reductant dithiothreitol (DTT) which triggers ER stress (Figure 2B, compare lanes 1–3 to lane 4). These findings suggest that no ER stress induction occurred during EMC1 depletion.
evidence: Supported by XBP1 splicing assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Depleting EMC1 significantly impairs SV40 infection.
source: Importantly, using this approach we found that depleting EMC1 significantly perturbed SV40 infection (Figure 2C, black bars).
evidence: Supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EMC1 knockdown markedly impairs BK PyV infection.
source: Moreover, EMC1 knockdown also markedly impaired infection by the human BK PyV (Figure 2C, open bars).
evidence: Supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EMC1 is broadly important for promoting PyV infection.
source: We conclude that EMC1 is broadly important for promoting PyV infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing EMC1 affects both SV40 and BK PyV infection.

claim: Knocking down other EMC subunits variably attenuates SV40 infection.
source: When the other 9 EMC subunits were individually knocked down (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), SV40 infection was attenuated variably (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by infection assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Some other EMC subunits may have roles during SV40 ER membrane penetration.
source: These findings raise the possibility that some of the other members of this complex may also have roles during SV40 ER membrane penetration, albeit with different levels of impact.
evidence: This is speculation based on the variable effects of knocking down different EMC subunits.

claim: Depleting EMC1 decreases SV40 levels in the cytosol.
source: Using this method, we found that depleting EMC1 potently decreased the VP1 level (which represents SV40) in the cytosol (Figure 3A, top panel; the VP1 band intensity in the cytosol is quantified in Figure 3B), indicating that EMC1 is crucial for promoting SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport.
evidence: Supported by membrane transport assay data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: EMC1 does not regulate SV40 trafficking from the plasma membrane to the ER.
source: Importantly, using this approach, we found that the level of ER-localized virus was the same between control and knockdown samples (Figure 3C, bottom panel; the VP1 band intensity in the ER-localized fraction is quantified in Figure 3D), demonstrating that EMC1 does not regulate SV40 trafficking from the plasma membrane to the ER.
evidence: Supported by ER arrival assay data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The block in SV40 cytosol arrival in EMC1-depleted cells reflects a specific role of EMC1 during viral ER-to-cytosol membrane penetration.
source: Hence, the block in SV40 arrival to the cytosol in EMC1-depleted cells reflects a specific role of EMC1 during the viral ER-to-cytosol membrane penetration step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing EMC1 affects cytosol arrival but not ER arrival.

claim: EMC1 depletion does not interfere with ER-to-cytosol transport of cholera toxin's CTA1 subunit.
source: As a negative control, silencing EMC1 did not interfere with ER-to-cytosol transport of another toxic agent cholera toxin's catalytic CTA1 subunit (Figure 3E), indicating that EMC1 depletion did not globally affect all ER membrane transport processes.
evidence: Supported by cholera toxin transport assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SV40 triggers FLAG-tagged wild type EMC1 to mobilize into foci structures.
source: We now find that SV40 similarly triggers FLAG-tagged wild type (WT) EMC1 (EMC1-FLAG) to mobilize into the foci structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ER membrane protein Sel1L does not mobilize into BAP31-positive foci structures.
source: By contrast, the ER membrane protein Sel1L (S/His-Sel1L) does not mobilize into the BAP31-positive foci structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), as previously reported (Bagchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citation.

claim: EMC1 executes a specific function in promoting SV40 ER membrane penetration.
source: Collectively, these results strongly suggest that EMC1 executes a specific function in promoting SV40 ER membrane penetration, consistent with its role in facilitating viral infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: EMC1's structural organization includes amino acids 1–21 as signal sequence (cleaved in the mature protein).
source: As a predicted type I transmembrane protein, EMC1's structural organization is expected to be as follows: amino acids 1–21 = signal sequence (cleaved in the mature protein), amino acids 22–958 = luminal domain, amino acids 959–979 = membrane domain, and amino acids 980–993 = cytosolic domain.
evidence: This is based on prediction of EMC1 structure.

claim: EMC1's structural organization includes amino acids 22–958 as luminal domain.
source: As a predicted type I transmembrane protein, EMC1's structural organization is expected to be as follows: amino acids 1–21 = signal sequence (cleaved in the mature protein), amino acids 22–958 = luminal domain, amino acids 959–979 = membrane domain, and amino acids 980–993 = cytosolic domain.
evidence: This is based on prediction of EMC1 structure.

claim: EMC1's structural organization includes amino acids 959–979 as membrane domain.
source: As a predicted type I transmembrane protein, EMC1's structural organization is expected to be as follows: amino acids 1–21 = signal sequence (cleaved in the mature protein), amino acids 22–958 = luminal domain, amino acids 959–979 = membrane domain, and amino acids 980–993 = cytosolic domain.
evidence: This is based on prediction of EMC1 structure.

claim: EMC1's structural organization includes amino acids 980–993 as cytosolic domain.
source: As a predicted type I transmembrane protein, EMC1's structural organization is expected to be as follows: amino acids 1–21 = signal sequence (cleaved in the mature protein), amino acids 22–958 = luminal domain, amino acids 959–979 = membrane domain, and amino acids 980–993 = cytosolic domain.
evidence: This is based on prediction of EMC1 structure.

claim: The negatively-charged amino acid D961 of EMC1 is highly conserved.
source: In this regard, despite predicted to be within the hydrophobic lipid bilayer, the negatively-charged amino acid D961 and polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 are highly conserved (Figure 4A), suggesting an important function.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 is highly conserved.
source: In this regard, despite predicted to be within the hydrophobic lipid bilayer, the negatively-charged amino acid D961 and polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 are highly conserved (Figure 4A), suggesting an important function.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants display an ER localization pattern similar to WT EMC1.
source: First, when transfected, these mutants displayed an ER localization pattern as the endogenous ER membrane protein BAP31, similar to transfected WT EMC1 (Figure 4B, compare second and third rows to the top row), indicating that D961A and T976A EMC1 are localized to the ER.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants are properly oriented in the ER membrane.
source: We found that both the D961A and T976A EMC1-FLAG mutants displayed a similar faster migration pattern as WT EMC1-FLAG when treated with this deglycosidase (Figure 4C, compare odd to even lanes), suggesting that the orientation of the EMC1 mutants is the same as WT EMC1.
evidence: Supported by deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants can bind to C18.
source: Third, we interrogated whether the EMC1 mutants can bind to EMC1's newly identified binding partner C18, and found that they did (Figure 4D, top panel, compare lane 2 to lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Adding back WT EMC1 to EMC1-depleted cells fully rescues SV40 infection.
source: Using this protocol, we found that adding back WT EMC1 to cells transfected with EMC1 siRNA #1 fully rescued SV40 infection (Figure 4E, compare third to second bar), unambiguously demonstrating that the block in SV40 infection and ER-to-cytosol transport due to EMC1 siRNA #1 treatment is specifically a result of depleting EMC1 and not to off-target effects.
evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Expressing T976A EMC1 mutant restores SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
source: Importantly, whereas expressing the T976A mutant also restored infection, expression of the D961A mutant did not (Figure 4E, compare fifth to fourth bars).
evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Expressing D961A EMC1 mutant does not restore SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
source: Importantly, whereas expressing the T976A mutant also restored infection, expression of the D961A mutant did not (Figure 4E, compare fifth to fourth bars).
evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: D961A EMC1 mutant binds to EMC3 transmembrane protein similar to WT EMC1.
source: It is unlikely that the D961A mutant failed to form a complex with the EMC because it binds to the EMC3 transmembrane protein, similar to WT EMC1 (Figure 4F, top panel, compare lane 3 to 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The D961 residue of EMC1 plays a specific and crucial role during SV40 infection.
source: These findings thus strongly suggest that the D961 residue of EMC1 plays a specific and crucial role during SV40 infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knockdown-rescue experiments.

claim: EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG truncation variant does not restore SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
source: We next asked if a FLAG-tagged EMC1 truncation variant that harbors the luminal domain and including residues up to D961 [EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG] is functional. We found that it was not because expressing this construct in EMC1 knocked down cells did not restore SV40 infection (Figure 4G), even though this construct displayed an ER expression pattern (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: An intact EMC1 membrane-spanning domain is required to promote SV40 ER membrane transport.
source: These findings indicate that an intact EMC1 membrane-spanning domain, presumably including residue D961, is required to promote SV40 ER membrane transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the truncation mutant experiments.

claim: SV40 crosses the ER membrane to reach the cytosol approximately 7–8 hours post infection.
source: We previously established that SV40 crosses the ER membrane to reach the cytosol approximately 7–8 hpi (Inoue and Tsai, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: EMC1 binds to SV40 at 7 hours post infection but not at 2 or 15 hours post infection.
source: In a time-course experiment, we found that in cells expressing WT EMC1-FLAG, precipitating EMC1 pulled down SV40 only at 7 but not 2 or 15 hpi (Figure 5A, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1 and 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation time-course data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: EMC1 binds to SV40 at approximately the time point when the virus is expected to penetrate the ER membrane.
source: Thus EMC1 binds to SV40 at approximately the time point when the virus is expected to penetrate the ER membrane; this interaction is lost later in the course of infection, perhaps reflecting a completion of SV40 cytosol arrival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-course binding data.

claim: D961A EMC1 mutant does not efficiently bind to SV40 compared to WT EMC1.
source: To test if D961 of EMC1 mediates the EMC1-SV40 interaction, we found that the D961A EMC1-FLAG mutant did not efficiently precipitate the virus when compared to WT EMC1-FLAG (Figure 5B, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1; the virus binding level is quantified in the bottom bar graph), suggesting that EMC1's D961 residue is critical in supporting virus binding.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SV40 co-precipitates poorly with truncated EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG construct compared to WT EMC1-FLAG during infection.
source: Additionally, as SV40 co-precipitates poorly with the truncated EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG construct when compared to WT EMC1-FLAG during infection (Figure 5C, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1; quantified in the bottom bar graph), the D961 residue must nonetheless act in the context of the rest of EMC1's transmembrane domain to fully support virus interaction.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt wash.
source: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt (0.5 M NaCl) wash (Figure 5D, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), in line with the idea that this binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
evidence: Supported by high salt wash experiment data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The EMC1-SV40 binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
source: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt (0.5 M NaCl) wash (Figure 5D, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), in line with the idea that this binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the salt sensitivity of the interaction.

claim: There is a strong correlation between EMC1's ability to interact with SV40 and promote infection.
source: These results establish a strong correlation between EMC1's ability to interact with the virus and promote infection, as the D961 residue is crucial to both processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Purified WT and D961A EMC1 samples do not contain other EMC subunits.
source: Mass spectrometry analyses of the WT and D961A EMC1 samples indicated that no other EMC subunits were present (not shown).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER.
source: Previous studies revealed that SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER (Inoue et al., 2015; Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012), an effect that can be mimicked in part by treating purified SV40 with DTT (which reduces the SV40 disulfide bonds) and EGTA (which removes calcium bound to the virus).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Treating purified SV40 with DTT and EGTA mimics ER-induced conformational changes.
source: Previous studies revealed that SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER (Inoue et al., 2015; Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012), an effect that can be mimicked in part by treating purified SV40 with DTT (which reduces the SV40 disulfide bonds) and EGTA (which removes calcium bound to the virus).
evidence: This is based on previous studies and the known effects of DTT and EGTA.

claim: EMC1 directly interacts with DTT/EGTA-treated SV40 but not untreated native SV40.
source: Indeed, when SV40 was incubated with either GFP-FLAG or WT EMC1-FLAG in the presence or absence of DTT/EGTA, pull down of EMC1 but not GFP precipitated SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), demonstrating a direct EMC1-SV40 interaction. By contrast, EMC1 did not interact with untreated native SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, lanes 3 and 4), suggesting that EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
source: Indeed, when SV40 was incubated with either GFP-FLAG or WT EMC1-FLAG in the presence or absence of DTT/EGTA, pull down of EMC1 but not GFP precipitated SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), demonstrating a direct EMC1-SV40 interaction. By contrast, EMC1 did not interact with untreated native SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, lanes 3 and 4), suggesting that EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential binding to treated vs untreated virus.

claim: D961A EMC1 mutant binds to DTT-EGTA destabilized SV40 less efficiently than WT EMC1 in vitro.
source: Moreover, using this in vitro approach, we found that the D961A EMC1 mutant binds to DTT-EGTA destabilized SV40 much less efficiently than WT EMC1 (Figure 5G, top panel, compare lane 1 to 2).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: EMC1 binds to VP1, but VP2 and VP3 also play important roles in supporting the EMC1-SV40 interaction.
source: To determine the viral components interacting with EMC1, we used VP1-containing viral-like-particles (VP1-VLP) devoid of VP2 and VP3 (Figure 5H, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1). Our results demonstrated that precipitating WT EMC1-FLAG pulled down less VP1-VLP when compared to WT SV40 (Figure 5H, top panel, compare lane 4 to 3; quantified in the right graph). These findings indicate that, although EMC1 binds to VP1, the internal proteins VP2 and VP3 also play important roles in supporting this interaction.
evidence: Supported by VP1-VLP binding assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Depleting EMC1 causes a portion of ER-localized SV40 to disassemble prematurely.
source: When ER-localized virus derived from control cells was analyzed, the virus was found in the bottom fraction (Figure 6A, top panel), suggesting that SV40 remains largely intact despite being partially destabilized in the ER. However, when ER-localized virus derived from EMC1-depleted cells was isolated and subjected to the same procedure, a distinct virus pool is present throughout the higher fractions corresponding to disassembled virus (Figure 6A, 2nd panel); these species likely reflect single, as well as oligomeric, VP1 pentamers. Hence a portion of ER-localized SV40 disassembles prematurely in EMC1-depleted cells.
evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EMC1 acts to stabilize SV40.
source: As disassembled ER-localized virus is found in the absence of EMC1, this finding suggests that EMC1 acts to stabilize SV40.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the disassembly assay results.

claim: Depleting SGTA or C18 does not cause premature SV40 disassembly.
source: To rule out the possibility that simply imposing a block in SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport is sufficient to cause viral premature disassembly, ER-localized virus derived from SGTA- or C18-depleted cells, which also display a strong impairment in SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport (Walczak et al., 2014; Goodwin et al., 2011), was isolated and subjected to the same procedure. However, no disassembled virus appeared in these samples (Figure 6A, 3rd and 4th panels).
evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The appearance of disassembled virus is not a general consequence of blocking ER membrane transport.
source: Thus, the appearance of the disassembled virus is not a general consequence of blocking ER membrane transport, but points to a specific role of EMC1 in conferring virus stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing EMC1 depletion to SGTA/C18 depletion.

claim: ER-localized SV40 from EMC1-depleted cells is more sensitive to proteolytic digestion by trypsin than virus from control cells.
source: We used a limited proteolysis approach as an independent strategy to further assess SV40's conformational state when EMC1 is depleted – this is a sensitive method used to detect subtle structural changes that may not be readily revealed by the sucrose gradient sedimentation assay. Using this approach, we found that ER-localized SV40 derived from EMC1-depleted cells is more sensitive to proteolytic digestion by trypsin than virus derived from control cells (Figure 6B, compare bottom to top panels).
evidence: Supported by limited proteolysis assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SV40 is structurally exposed when EMC1 is absent.
source: These findings indicate that SV40 is structurally exposed when EMC1 is absent, supporting the sucrose sedimentation data demonstrating that the viral particle experiences premature disassembly without EMC1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteolysis assay results.

claim: EMC1 protects SV40 against DTT/EGTA-induced disassembly in vitro.
source: However, if EMC1 was simultaneously incubated in the presence of the destabilizing agents (DTT/EGTA), a significant pool of SV40 sediments to the bottom fraction, representing intact virus (Figure 6C, third panel). This finding suggests that EMC1 protects SV40 against disassembly, supporting the notion that it acts to stabilize the virus.
evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WT EMC1 cannot confer protection against viral disassembly once the virus has disassembled.
source: However, when SV40 was pre-treated with DTT/EGTA and then incubated with WT EMC1, the virus level that sediments to the bottom fraction decreased significantly compared to when WT EMC1 was simultaneously incubated with DTT/EGTA (Figure 6C, compare fourth to third panel). This result demonstrates that WT EMC1 cannot confer protection against viral disassembly once the virus has disassembled.
evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: D961A EMC1 mutant does not provide strong protection against DTT/EGTA-induced SV40 disassembly compared to WT EMC1.
source: Importantly, the D961A EMC1 mutant did not provide strong protection against DTT/EGTA-induced SV40 disassembly when compared to WT EMC1 (Figure 6C, compare fifth to third panel).
evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WT EMC1 protected more than 66% of SV40 against DTT/EGTA-triggered disassembly whereas D961A mutant protected approximately 18%.
source: When quantified, WT EMC1 protected more than 66% of SV40 against DTT/EGTA-triggered disassembly whereas the mutant EMC1 protected approximately 18% of the virus against disassembly, where virus in fractions 1–6 represents disassembled virus and those in fractions 7–9 represents largely intact particles (Ravindran et al., 2015) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cell-based results coupled with in vitro reconstitution experiments strongly argue that EMC1 imparts a stabilizing force to SV40 during ER membrane penetration.
source: Hence our cell-based results coupled with the in vitro reconstitution experiments strongly argue that EMC1 imparts a stabilizing force to the virus during the ER membrane penetration process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Hsc70 cannot capture SV40 when EMC1 is downregulated.
source: We reasoned that a prematurely disassembled virus might not assume the proper conformation to properly engage the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery that normally extracts SV40 into the cytosol - this would explain why EMC1 depletion blocks cytosol entry of the virus. To test this possibility, we first asked if Hsc70 is able to capture SV40 when EMC1 is downregulated. Cells expressing S-tagged Hsc70 (Hsc70-S) were transfected with either scrambled or EMC1 #1 siRNA. When Hsc70-S was affinity purified from the resulting WCE, SV40 was only pulled down using extracts from control but not EMC1-depleted cells (Figure 7A, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knocking down EMC1 does not affect the integrity of the Hsc70-SGTA interaction.
source: By contrast, endogenous SGTA was precipitated under both conditions (Figure 7A, second panel, compare lane 1 to 2), suggesting that knocking down EMC1 did not affect the integrity of the Hsc70-SGTA interaction.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: EMC1 knockdown prevents SGTA from binding to SV40.
source: A similar result was found for SGTA: EMC1 knockdown prevents (transfected) SGTA from binding to SV40 (Figure 7A, top panel, compare lane 4 to 3), but not to endogenous Hsc70 (Figure 7A, second panel, compare lane 4 to 3).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: EMC1 is required to allow SV40 to engage the cytosolic extraction machinery.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that EMC1 is required to allow SV40 to engage the cytosolic extraction machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding experiments with Hsc70 and SGTA.

claim: The extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence.
source: However, we found that precipitating C18-S pulled down endogenous Hsc70 and SGTA regardless of EMC1's presence (Figure 7B, top and second panels, compare lane 2 to 1); silencing EMC1 also preserved the interaction between SGTA and Hsp105 with another J-protein B14 (not shown). Hence, as the extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence, the simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly, thereby precluding its interaction with this machinery.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly.
source: Hence, as the extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence, the simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly, thereby precluding its interaction with this machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing extraction machinery localization is preserved but virus binding is lost.

claim: Virus stabilization can serve a crucial function during viral entry.
source: Host-encoded forces stabilizing a viral particle are generally exploited to support viral assembly (Prange et al., 1999; Cobbold et al., 2001). The resulting assembled virus in turn exits the host cell to cause the next round of infection. By contrast, we report here that virus stabilization can also serve a crucial function during viral entry.
evidence: This is a novel conclusion drawn from the current study in contrast to previous knowledge.

claim: EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, deploying its D961 residue to engage membrane-embedded SV40 and promote ER membrane penetration.
source: Specifically, we found that the largest component of the ER membrane complex EMC called EMC1 executes an essential role during SV40 ER-to-cytosol membrane transport, a decisive entry step for this non-enveloped virus. Our data strongly suggest that EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, deploying its highly conserved D961 residue in order to engage the membrane-embedded SV40 and promote the ER membrane penetration event (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental data.

claim: D961 residue likely functions within the membrane-spanning domain or at the membrane border.
source: This residue likely functions within the membrane-spanning domain (or at the membrane border), and must act in concert with the rest of EMC1's transmembrane domain to accomplish its role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural predictions and functional data.

claim: EMC1's interaction stabilizes the overall SV40 architecture within the ER lipid bilayer or at the earliest phase of membrane insertion.
source: Because membrane-penetrating SV40 is partially destabilized, EMC1's interaction stabilizes the overall viral architecture either within the ER lipid bilayer or at the earliest phase of the membrane insertion process.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Stabilization maintains SV40 in a transport-competent state, enabling recognition by the cytosolic Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 extraction machinery.
source: Importantly, stabilization maintains the virus in a transport-competent state, enabling it to be recognized by the cytosolic Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 extraction machinery, which completes the membrane transport process by ejecting the virus into the cytosol.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing stabilization is required for extraction machinery engagement.

claim: Coordinated interplay between destabilization and stabilization drives PyV entry.
source: Thus, ironically, while host encoded forces that destabilize SV40 are known to promote viral ER-to-cytosol transport (Ravindran et al., 2015), an opposing force that stabilizes SV40 appears to play an equally important role during this step. The concept that coordinated interplay between destabilization and stabilization drive PyV entry may have broad implications in illuminating other viral entry mechanisms, including enveloped viruses.
evidence: This is the main conceptual conclusion of the study.

claim: Host factors stabilize the HIV viral capsid to prevent premature uncoating during entry.
source: For instance, in destabilizing the enveloped virus HIV during entry, host factors also stabilize the viral capsid in a concerted manner in order to prevent its premature uncoating, which otherwise prevents infection (Guth and Sodroski, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on HIV.

claim: Coordinated destabilization-stabilization is an important concept during viral entry.
source: Thus, there is clearly a precedent for the hypothesis that coordinated destabilization-stabilization is an important (yet poorly-explored) concept during viral entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings to HIV entry.

claim: EMC1 recognizes positively-charged residues exposed in the membrane-inserted SV40.
source: Our finding that EMC1's D961 residue is essential for binding to and stabilizing the partially destabilized SV40 suggests that EMC1 recognizes positively-charged residues exposed in the membrane-inserted virus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the charge properties of D961 and the binding data.

claim: EMC1's transmembrane domain might function as a 'sensor', recognizing exposure of aberrant membrane-spanning residues in substrates.
source: Hence, EMC1's transmembrane domain might function as a 'sensor', recognizing exposure of aberrant membrane-spanning residues in substrates.
evidence: This is speculation about EMC1's general mechanism of action.

claim: VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus.
source: Because VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus (Magnuson et al., 2005; Norkin et al., 2002; Rainey-Barger et al., 2007; Kuksin and Norkin, 2012; Daniels et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2011), it is tempting to speculate that despite the overall hydrophobic nature of these internal proteins, positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
source: Because VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus (Magnuson et al., 2005; Norkin et al., 2002; Rainey-Barger et al., 2007; Kuksin and Norkin, 2012; Daniels et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2011), it is tempting to speculate that despite the overall hydrophobic nature of these internal proteins, positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
evidence: This is speculation based on the VP2/VP3 exposure and the D961 charge.

claim: A VP1-VLP lacking VP2 and VP3 displayed less efficient binding to EMC1 compared to WT SV40.
source: This idea is supported by our data that a VP1-VLP lacking VP2 and VP3 displayed less efficient binding to EMC1 when compared to WT SV40 that harbors these internal proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Positively-charged residues exposed in VP1 may also represent the contact point with EMC1.
source: Positively-charged residues exposed in the coat protein VP1 may also represent the contact point with EMC1, since VP1-VLP appears to be sufficient in providing some level of interaction with this transmembrane protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on the VP1-VLP binding data.

claim: EMC1 stabilization might reflect a passive process of shielding exposed charges on SV40.
source: The postulated exposure of the positively-charged residues in SV40 might cause electrostatic repulsion between the viral particles that would destabilize its structural integrity. Furthermore, displaying positive charges on the viral surface within the hydrophobic ER lipid bilayer creates a highly energetically unfavorable condition. Thus stabilization might reflect a rather passive process in which EMC1 simply shields these charges.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of stabilization.

claim: EMC1-dependent stabilization may be an active process involving recruitment of EMC1's luminal domain to provide VP1 inter-pentamer interactions.
source: Alternatively, EMC1-dependent stabilization may be a more complex active process. For instance, upon recognizing exposure of aberrant residues in membrane-embedded SV40 via EMC1's transmembrane domain, EMC1's luminal domain might subsequently be recruited to provide VP1 inter-pentamer interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism of stabilization.

claim: In infected cells devoid of EMC1, different prematurely disassembled VP1 species, likely corresponding to single and oligomeric VP1 pentamers, are generated.
source: Our sucrose sedimentation analyses revealed that in infected cells devoid of EMC1, different prematurely disassembled VP1 species, likely corresponding to single and oligomeric VP1 pentamers, are generated (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EMC1 stabilizes inter-pentamer interactions.
source: This observation suggests that EMC1 stabilizes inter-pentamer interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the disassembly pattern observed.

claim: EMC1 may exist as oligomers that enable each EMC1 monomer to crosslink to an individual VP1 molecule belonging to different pentamers.
source: To enhance VP1 inter-pentamer interactions, EMC1 may exists as oligomers that enable each EMC1 monomer to crosslink to an individual VP1 molecule belonging to different pentamers.
evidence: This is speculation about how EMC1 might stabilize inter-pentamer interactions.

claim: EMC1 may operate in both manners to shield exposed charges and to reinforce interactions between pentamers.
source: Clearly these two possibilities do not have to be mutually exclusive – EMC1 may operate in both manners to shield the presumed exposed charges and to reinforce interactions between the pentamers.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of EMC1 action.

claim: Addition of DTT and EGTA to purified SV40 generates VP1 pentamers.
source: In our in vitro analyses, addition of DTT and EGTA also generated VP1 pentamers (Figure 6B), whose formation can be largely suppressed by addition of purified EMC1; DTT likely mimics viral disulfide bond reduction that occurs in the ER lumen (Inoue et al., 2015), whereas EGTA may imitate loss of Ca2+ from the membrane-embedded virus when it is exposed to the low Ca2+ in the cytosol, as previously hypothesized (Schelhaas et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citations.

claim: In EMC1-depleted cells, the virus does not engage the cytosolic extraction machinery composed of the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 complex.
source: Why might stabilization of membrane-embedded SV40 by EMC1 be important for membrane transport? Our studies revealed that in EMC1-depleted cells, the virus does not engage the cytosolic extraction machinery composed of the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 complex (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citations.

claim: The extraction machinery cannot recognize a prematurely disassembled virus in the membrane, but a largely intact virus is required for productive interaction.
source: This finding suggests that the extraction machinery cannot recognize a prematurely disassembled virus in the membrane, but that a largely intact virus is instead required for productive interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding experiments.

claim: Once the extraction machinery recognizes membrane-inserted SV40, it has the capacity to disassemble the virus.
source: Interestingly, our experiments previously suggested that once the extraction machinery recognizes the membrane-inserted SV40, it has the capacity to disassemble the virus (Ravindran et al., 2015) – we postulated that this disassembly reaction might be coupled to the extraction reaction.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Initial recognition of the viral particle by the extraction machinery requires the virus to remain relatively intact.
source: Thus, while initial recognition of the viral particle by the extraction machinery requires the virus to remain relatively intact, subsequent to recognition, this machinery disassembles it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current and previous findings.

claim: In humans, the EMC is composed of 10 subunits (EMC1-EMC10).
source: In humans, the EMC is composed of 10 subunits (EMC1-EMC10), with EMC1 representing the largest component (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: EMC1 is sufficient to function as a molecular chaperone.
source: Because our findings demonstrate that EMC1 is sufficient to function as a molecular chaperone, whether other EMC subunits can also act in a similar role or execute completely different functions remain to be clarified.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing purified EMC1 can stabilize SV40.

claim: The EMC was initially identified in yeast.
source: The EMC was initially identified in yeast, although its precise function was not fully clarified (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The EMC was proposed to function within ERAD.
source: This complex was proposed to function within an ER quality control process called ERAD, in which misfolded ER proteins are targeted to the cytosol for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation (Ruggiano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Different EMC subunits physically associate with other components of the ERAD machinery.
source: This possibility is consistent with the finding demonstrating that different EMC subunits physically associate with other components of the ERAD machinery (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ER-to-cytosol transport of a misfolded substrate during ERAD is highly reminiscent of the pathway SV40 experiences during its ER membrane transport.
source: Strikingly, ER-to-cytosol transport of a misfolded substrate during ERAD is highly reminiscent of the pathway SV40 experiences during its ER membrane transport.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between ERAD and SV40 transport pathways.

claim: The EMC supports biosynthesis of multi-pass transmembrane proteins such as the ionotropic acetylcholine receptor and rhodopsin.
source: Another related ER quality control function attributed to the EMC is its ability to support biosynthesis of multi-pass transmembrane proteins, such as the ionotropic acetylcholine receptor (Richard et al., 2013) and rhodopsin (Satoh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The EMC appears to serve as a transmembrane chaperone, promoting stabilization of membrane protein folding-intermediates.
source: In these cases, the EMC appears to serve as a transmembrane chaperone, promoting the stabilization of the membrane protein folding-intermediates.
evidence: This is based on previous studies of EMC function in membrane protein biosynthesis.

claim: The EMC plays a critical role during flavivirus (including Zika, Dengue, and West Nile virus) infection.
source: For example, a series of recent reports suggest that the EMC plays a critical role during flavivirus (including Zika, Dengue, and West Nile virus) infection (Ma et al., 2015; Savidis et al., 2016; Marceau et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Replication and assembly of flaviviruses are events associated with the ER membrane.
source: As a wealth of literature has established that replication and assembly of flaviviruses are events in their life cycle associated with the ER membrane (Ravindran et al., 2016), it is perhaps not surprising that this ER membrane protein complex might exert a role during their infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The molecular basis by which the EMC controls flavivirus infection remains completely unknown.
source: However, despite these reports, the molecular basis by which the EMC controls flavivirus infection remains completely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutant EMC1 alleles are strongly associated with various human neurodevelopmental disorders, including global developmental delay and cerebellar atrophy.
source: Finally, mutant EMC1 alleles were recently found to be strongly associated with various human neurodevelopmental disorders, including global developmental delay and cerebellar atrophy (Harel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.
